digest.intro: The Riemann Hypothesis fell. Also: everything else happened simultaneously.

items.title: The Riemann Hypothesis is proved — and machine-checked
items.blurb: Levent Alpöge, an Anthropic mathematician working with Claude, released a Lean 4 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis yesterday — 17 million lines of code, now compiled and verified correct by dozens of independent researchers within 24 hours. The community has certified all four criteria: correct statement, clean compilation, proof of the right theorem, and no dependency outside Mathlib. The deepest open problem in mathematics, standing since 1859, is closed — and the closure was machine-checked before most people woke up.

items.title: The four-page announcement, in Alpöge's own words
items.blurb: The primary source is a brief remark document where Alpöge sketches the Fourier-analytic approach, theta lifts, and an analogy with Stepanov's elementary proof of the Weil conjectures — the kind of analogy that, in retrospect, makes you wonder why no one saw it sooner. The PDF is the actual mathematical argument before it became a news story; worth reading even if the machinery is unfamiliar, because the structure of the insight is legible.

items.title: Meanwhile: a second independent GRH claim dropped the same day, then ran into trouble
items.blurb: While Alpöge's proof was being verified, mathematician Alessandro Masullo — working entirely without AI, with months of feedback from Brian Conrad — also released a claimed proof of GRH on the same day, in an urgent pre-announcement from an AMS board meeting. Within eight hours, multiple mathematicians reported potential gaps, identified with the help of AI models. Two simultaneous independent claims after 167 years of silence is not coincidence; something shifted in the mathematical environment this year.

items.title: Musk playing satellite politics: SpaceX Starshield, Ukraine, and a congressional threat
items.blurb: House Intelligence Committee chair-designate Jim Himes sent SpaceX a letter warning that unilateral modifications to Starshield service in Ukraine — cutting drone connectivity during active Russian attacks — calls into question every US government contract with the company. This is the privatization-of-military-infrastructure problem made concrete: a single founder's decision can interrupt a nation's battlefield communications, and Congress has limited leverage over a classified contract. The chickens are roosting.

items.title: Iran dirty-bomb plot, Denmark expels Russian attaché: two tripwires live simultaneously
items.blurb: Trump threatened military action against Iran over a reported dirty-bomb plot targeting Washington, while Denmark ordered Russia's defense attaché out within seven days and halted non-essential Russian visas — Foreign Minister Rasmussen's phrase was 'enough is enough.' Both the Iran escalation and the European-Russian diplomatic rupture are moving simultaneously, which is the actual story: these are not separate news cycles.

items.title: 2 million canaries in the AI supply chain — and a lot of them sang
items.blurb: Researcher HD Moore seeded 2 million unique, never-previously-used credential tokens into prompts sent through AI routing services like OpenRouter and Vercel — brokers that arbitrage inference across providers by cheapest price — and monitored his own infrastructure for any activity. The canaries sang: sensitive data leaked across the supply chain at scale, with credentials being actively exploited. If you use any AI tool that isn't a direct API call to a named model, your prompts may be traveling through infrastructure with no accountability.

items.title: METR's AI trajectory graph, updated — where the exponential holds and where it doesn't
items.blurb: METR's updated time-horizon plot — the one showing frontier models doubling their completable task-length every four months — now includes longer-horizon and more open-ended tasks, and the finding is clarifying: exponential improvement holds for verifiable tasks (coding, math), but models underperform on tasks requiring judgment where success is hard to measure automatically. The gap between 'can it pass the test' and 'can it do the thing' is the most important unresolved question in applied AI right now.

items.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains — the same week an Anthropic researcher proved the Riemann Hypothesis
items.blurb: Anthropic's record IPO — the largest in history — dropped 9% on its second day of trading, dragging Nvidia down 14% and erasing $4 trillion in Nasdaq market cap for the week. The timing is almost too perfect: the same company whose researcher just proved the Riemann Hypothesis watched its stock head toward its IPO price while Asian markets posted their worst week since 2020. Whether that's irony or information depends on your theory of what AI is actually for.

items.title: What peahens actually want — and what it means for how taste works
items.blurb: The standard story is that peacock tails are fitness signals — peahens choose the most symmetrical tail because it correlates with genetic health. A new chapter in evolutionary biology argues that's too reductive: peahens may be selecting for perceptual and aesthetic complexity itself, suggesting that taste in biological systems emerges from something closer to pleasure in sensory richness than rational fitness calculation. Darwin actually believed this — that animals experience beauty — and it was quietly suppressed by his successors. If true, aesthetic preference formation is not a shortcut for something else; it's the thing.

items.title: What do stem-like T cells have to do with why Type 1 diabetes never stops?
items.blurb: UF Diabetes Institute researchers publishing in the Journal of Clinical Investigation identified a population of stem-like T cells in human pancreas-draining lymph nodes that appear to continuously self-renew and replenish the autoimmune attack — which is why T1D doesn't resolve the way other immune responses do. 'That is what is perpetuating autoimmunity as a chronic condition,' said lead researcher Todd Brusko. It's preliminary in the sense that it opens drug target pathways rather than closing them, but it's the first mechanistic explanation for the chronicity that's been confirmed in human tissue.

facts.fact: The Lean 4 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is 17 million lines of code — compiled and independently verified by dozens of researchers within 24 hours of release.

Two independent claimed proofs of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis were announced on the same day — November 20, 2026 — the first time the problem has had even one serious candidate proof in 167 years.

HD Moore seeded 2 million unique credential canaries into AI routing service prompts; none of the credentials had ever been used before, and his infrastructure received unauthorized requests — proving live exploitation of leaked prompt data at scale.

Stem cells grown on a platform that mechanically mimics the rhythmic stretching of breathing produced extracellular vesicles with 3.3 times more antifibrotic microRNA than cells grown in static culture.

Anthropic's IPO was the largest in history, yet its shares fell 9% on day two — coinciding with the week a company researcher proved the Riemann Hypothesis — erasing roughly $4 trillion in Nasdaq market cap.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film-essay that moves between Japan, Guinea-Bissau, and Iceland interrogating how images build collective memory — the systems of ritual, forgetting, and time are the actual subject. If you like rabbit holes that dissolve the boundary between cinema and essay, nothing goes deeper.

art_picks.title: Homosapiens — The Love Album
art_picks.creator: Ólafur Elíasson
art_picks.why: Elíasson's installations consistently ask how built environments shape perception and feedback into identity. His studio archive and practice site rewards deep reading — the work sits exactly at the edge where physics, craftsmanship, and phenomenology collapse into each other.

art_picks.title: Maxinquaye
art_picks.creator: Tricky
art_picks.why: One of the great examples of a system built from pure texture and dread — trip-hop as a kind of psychological architecture. Obsessive craft at the production level, with identity and gender as the hidden load-bearing structure underneath. It still sounds like nothing else.

events.name: Leonora Carrington & Cecilia Vicuña
events.why: Pairing a surrealist mythmaker with a Chilean poet-artist who works in precarious fiber systems — this is a show about ritual, cosmology, and the kind of image-making that functions as belief before it functions as art.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt — LAST WEEK
events.venue: MoMA Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, 11 W 53rd St, Manhattan
events.why: A neural network trained on fMRI brain-scan data generates hallucinatory images on freestanding screens in the sculpture garden, mutated in real time by visitors' gazes and simulated cancer-cell data — this is the question of machine cognition made physically walkable, closing next weekend.

events.name: Einstein on the Beach — 50th Anniversary Concert (TONIGHT)
events.venue: BAM Howard Gilman Opera House, 30 Lafayette Ave, Brooklyn
events.why: The Philip Glass Ensemble performs the score that permanently rewired opera and minimalism, with an installation by Es Devlin built into the evening — tonight is the final performance of this run.

events.name: Iris van Herpen: Sculpting the Senses
events.why: 140+ couture garments conceived with architects, bioengineers, and astrophysicists unfold across eleven thematic chapters — the exhibition reconstructs her Amsterdam atelier so you can look down microscopes and handle the fabric, which is as close to a design-research document as fashion gets.

events.name: Arthur Jafa in Conversation with Tyler Cowen
events.why: Jafa makes films that treat Black visual culture as a living technical system — putting him in dialogue with an economist obsessed with cultural transmission should produce exactly the kind of category-collision worth your two hours.
